children: Metcalfe's Law says that the value of a network is proportional to the square of how many members are in that network
A model for calculating bitcoin's value has worked well to inform investors when the cryptocurrency is overbought or oversold. Now, the price is just right.
Bitcoin once again is trading for fair value, according to a model based on Metcalfe's Law.

I say "once again" because many of bitcoin's true believers treated the cryptocurrency's summer low as nothing more than a temporary aberration. When bitcoin (BTCUSD) subsequently rallied to nearly $87,000, those true believers triumphantly declared that a new bull market was under way.
It was not to be. Bitcoin fell over this past weekend to slightly above $62,000 - just as the Metcalfe's Law model expected. The model calculates that bitcoin's current fair value is around $62,500.
I have written about this model several times previously. Metcalfe's Law says that the value of a network is proportional to the square of how many members are in that network.

Claude Erb, a former commodities portfolio manager at TCW Group, introduced me nearly seven years ago to how to apply this model to bitcoin's valuation. As you can see from the accompanying chart, the model has worked remarkably well in real time since then - with its calculation in effect acting as a magnet pulling bitcoin back whenever it deviated significantly.

As I have stressed on the prior occasions I have written about this model, however, it undeniably has theoretical flaws. Some investors own more than one bitcoin, for example, and in other cases bitcoins have been lost forever. So there isn't an exact 1-to-1 correspondence between the number of bitcoins that have been mined up until this point and how many members are in the bitcoin "network."
Furthermore, the close historical fit between bitcoin's price and the calculation of the Metcalfe's Law model doesn't prove that it is right or true. Correlation is not causation, after all.

Nevertheless, the model's track record suggests that cryptocurrency investors should pay attention to it. It certainly has done a better job up until now than competing models - some of which had predicted bitcoin would already be trading for more than $1 million.
In an email earlier this week, Erb commented that "bitcoin's price trajectory looks a bit like a rocket running out of fuel."

Another implication of the Metcalfe's Law model is that bitcoin's long-term return will be only moderately positive. That's because its supply is algorithmically set not to exceed 21 million (in the year 2140), versus just over 20 million currently. Assuming the model's prediction is correct, bitcoin's price in 2140 will be around $120,000 - representing an annualized gain of 0.6% from its current price. (Erb recently posted a paper on the Social Science Research Network that discusses what the model means for long-term investors.)
